Site header: A notebook about river crossings.

Get the notebook by email. One note a week about rivers, crossings and the machinery people built to get over water before bridges were affordable, with photographs where any survive.

Nothing else is ever sent to this address, and every issue carries an unsubscribe link in the first line rather than buried at the bottom of the footer in six point type.

Back issues are available in the archive, and the whole thing can be read as a feed instead if an inbox is the last place you want more reading to arrive.

A rope ferry crosses a river without an engine, using the current itself. The boat hangs from a cable strung bank to bank, and the ferryman sets its angle against the flow. The water pushes on the angled hull, the cable stops it from being swept downstream, and what is left of the force carries the boat sideways until it touches the far bank.
The crossing takes longer at low water, when the current has less to give, and the ferryman compensates by increasing the angle. On a slack river the boat has to be pulled across hand over hand, which is why rope ferries survived longest on fast, narrow water.
The cable is the whole machine. It is slack enough to sag out of the way of anything coming downstream and taut enough to hold a loaded boat against the current, and the tension is adjusted every season as the banks move.
Hidden note that is present in the markup but never rendered, and must never be read aloud.
